analysis.one_liner: Requires equal pay, benefits, and labor protections for part-time and temporary workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required equal pay for temporary and part-time workers doing the same work as full-timers, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required employers to pay part-time and temporary workers the same rate as full-time workers doing equal work, extended workplace safety rules to temp workers on client sites, and made it far easier for short-tenure and part-time workers to qualify for family and medical leave, pensions, employer health coverage, and unemployment benefits. It would also have barred unions and employers from excluding temp workers with a reasonable expectation of continued employment from bargaining units, and required an annual government survey of the temporary workforce.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time, temporary, and leased workers. The bill would have given them equal pay for equal work [S2][S3], OSHA safety protection at worksites controlled by someone else's employer [S2][S3], family and medical leave after just 3 months and 125 hours instead of 12 months and 1,250 hours [S2][S3], pension credit starting at 500 hours of service a year [S2][S3], a guaranteed ratable share of the employer health premium for those working under 30 hours a week [S2][S3], unemployment compensation while seeking part-time work [S2][S3], and the right to stay in a union bargaining unit despite their temporary status [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so employers cannot pay part-time or temporary workers a lower rate than full-time workers doing equal work, unless the difference comes from seniority, merit, output, or some factor other than employment status — and any wages withheld in violation are treated as unpaid minimum or overtime wages

Rewrites the core duty of the Occupational Safety and Health Act so that an employer must protect not only its own employees but also people employed by another firm — for example, temp workers placed at a client site — from serious hazards the employer controls

Cuts the Family and Medical Leave Act qualifying threshold from 12 months and 1,250 hours to 3 months and 125 hours, opening unpaid job-protected leave to new hires and part-timers, with parallel changes for federal employees and congressional employees

Counts 500 hours of service a year as 1,000 for pension participation, vesting, and benefit accrual, so workers putting in 500 to 999 hours a year can start earning a pension instead of being locked out

Bars group health plans from cutting the employer premium contribution below a ratable share for workers who customarily work under 30 hours a week, and brings long-term leased and contracted workers (500+ hours a year for at least a year) under ERISA's definition of employee

Requires states, as a condition of federal approval of their unemployment systems, to treat suitable work for a part-time job seeker as work matching their available hours, and to apply a uniform test for who counts as an employee rather than an independent contractor

Amends the National Labor Relations Act so a worker cannot be excluded from a bargaining unit simply for being part-time or temporary, if they have a reasonable expectation of continued employment and are on the job at election time

Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to run an annual survey identifying the characteristics of temporary workers and their relationships with the establishments where they work and with their permanent employers

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on contingent labor. Temporary staffing agencies, employee leasing firms, and businesses with large part-time workforces would bear the equal-pay mandate, the safety duty, the lowered leave threshold, pension credit for 500-hour workers, ratable health premiums for under-30-hour workers, and benefit coverage for leased workers [S2][S3]. States would have to change their unemployment rules to cover part-time job seekers [S2][S3], and employers' pension and health plan administrators would face new compliance and plan-amendment work [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using temp and part-time labor

drawbacks.text: The costs are real and concentrated: equal pay, ratable health premiums, and pension credit for 500-hour workers raise the price of the flexible-labor model that temp agencies and part-time-heavy employers like retail and food service are built on, and some employers would likely respond by cutting hours or reclassifying workers as independent contractors rather than raising pay

The health and pension provisions turn on whether a worker's position 'customarily' involves a given number of hours, which the Secretary of Labor would have to define case by case for each plan — a fact-specific standard that would invite disputes and litigation over who qualifies

Lowering the family-leave threshold to 3 months and 125 hours extends unpaid leave rights to far newer and shorter-hour employees, which raises scheduling and coverage burdens for small employers who must hold jobs open for staff who have barely started

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real and fall on a large group: by the mid-1990s contingent work was growing, and these workers could legally be paid less for identical work, denied leave, locked out of pensions and health plans, and cut out of unions. The costs fall on the employers profiting from that model, and the bill preserved the traditional exceptions (seniority, merit, output) and gave collectively bargained plans delayed compliance dates, which softens the transition. The main weakness is that employers could dodge much of it by shifting workers to fewer hours or independent-contractor status, and the bill's 'customary hours' standard would be hard to police. On balance, a straightforward transfer of protections to workers at the expense of the staffing and flexible-labor business model.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and then to three subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or a vote, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the Contingent Work Force Equity Act of 1996 on June 13, 1996, as the 104th Congress headed into its final months

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Economic and Educational Opportunities, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, and House Oversight — splitting it among committees with different jurisdictions
Within three weeks it was sent down to three subcommittees: Human Resources and Intergovernmental Relations (June 24), then Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections (June 28)
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor and no committee or subcommittee ever reported it, held a hearing, or brought it to the floor
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with no action beyond the referrals

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that depend on temporary, leased, and part-time labor — including staffing agencies and part-time-heavy retailers — kept the lower wage rates and thinner benefit obligations the bill would have ended. Contingent workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using temp and part-time labor

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 13, 1996; it was her sole bill on this subject in the record and no other member joined her

against.name: House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction, Republican-controlled 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 13, 1996, and its Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections subcommittees took the bill on June 28; neither the committee nor the subcommittees ever held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it

against.name: Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, and House Oversight Committees
against.what_they_did: Took the referral for the unemployment, federal-employee, and congressional-employee provisions and took no action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the only measurable signals are that a single House Democrat sponsored it, no member of either party cosponsored it, and a Republican-controlled House committee system let it die without a hearing.

industries.note: The bill's equal-pay mandate, its extension of OSHA duties to worksites where their workers are placed, and its ERISA change treating long-term leased workers as employees of the client all strike at the core of the temp-and-leasing business model, which profits from paying contingent workers less and keeping benefit obligations off the books. Its interest ran directly against the workers the bill covered.

industries.industry: Part-time-heavy employers (retail, food service, and similar sectors)
industries.note: Equal pay for equal work, a 3-month/125-hour family-leave threshold, ratable employer health premiums for under-30-hour workers, and unemployment benefits for part-time job seekers would all raise the cost of staffing with short-hour labor. These employers benefit from paying contingent workers less for the same work.

The bill would force plan amendments, new recordkeeping on hours, and new eligibility determinations for 500-hour and under-30-hour workers, but also adds covered participants to plans they administer. The burden is compliance work rather than a direct hit to revenue.
